title: Washing and shrouds
hook: the body is washed and dressed in plain white shrouds, the same for everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chevra kadisha, and your line was the holy society: true kindness that can't be repaid. Today, what the holy society actually does.

Families were running away from their own dead. That's the scene the Talmud describes. Burial had become so expensive, with fine clothes and costly display, that for some, the cost of a funeral was harder to bear than the death itself. Some relatives would leave the body and flee. Then Rabban Gamliel, a leader of his generation, made a request about his own funeral: bury me in plain linen. The people followed him, and carried out their own dead in linen too.
screen: `FAMILIES FLED THEIR DEAD.` → `BURY ME IN PLAIN LINEN.` → `THE PEOPLE FOLLOWED.`

segments.voice: Before that plain linen comes tahara, purification: the ritual washing of the body, done by the holy society. The body is cleaned gently and thoroughly, the face kept covered and only the part being washed uncovered, out of modesty. Then water is poured over the whole body in a continuous flow. Members say verses and prayers as they work, and in some communities, at the end, they say: tehorah hi, she is pure, or tahor hu, he is pure. Then the shrouds, called tachrichim: plain white garments, usually linen or cotton, sewn by hand, with no pockets, and in some traditions no buttons or knots. A Yiddish saying goes: shrouds have no pockets. You take nothing with you. A rabbi and a cab driver, a philanthropist and a person who died with nothing: dressed alike. That goes back to Rabban Gamliel. Equality in death wasn't an accident; it was a decision, made so no family would be shamed. Some men are also wrapped in their own tallit, the prayer shawl, with one fringe cut. In the book of Job, after losing everything, Job says: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither." Tahara treats the body almost as a newborn is treated: washed by others, wrapped by others, held by others.
screen: `WASHED WITH MODESTY.` · `PLAIN WHITE SHROUDS, NO POCKETS.` · `RABBI AND CAB DRIVER, ALIKE.` · `NAKED CAME I.` · then, large: `EVERYONE EQUAL IN DEATH.`

segments.voice: Look at what you're wearing, and notice what in it says something about you: a brand, a ring, a badge, a style. Without judging any of it, ask: if all of this were replaced with one plain white garment, what would still be me? If you pray, you can say the line from Job slowly, or sit in silence.
Tahara. Purification: the washing of the body, the flow of water, and plain white shrouds, the same for everyone. Today's word.
Your line: everyone equal in death. No family shamed, no one set apart. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Before a traditional Jewish burial, members of the chevra kadisha perform tahara, washing the body with care and pouring water over it, then dress it in simple white shrouds called tachrichim; some men are also wrapped in their tallit.

chat.says: Why are Jewish people buried in plain white shrouds instead of their nice clothes?
options: Tachrichim are the same for everyone, so no family is shamed; you take nothing along.
It's only a money-saving rule from funeral homes; the tradition says nothing.
Plain white is only for rabbis and very pious people, as a special honor.
